reasons: No error-handling step is defined here, so failures show the framework default response.
The cross-origin setting has no restrictions, which should be reviewed before the API handles sensitive data.
No tests for this file are visible.

terms.meaning: a widely used library that makes it easier to build web servers
a step that every request passes through before it reaches the final route
a rule that matches a web address and sends the request to the right code
a browser rule that decides which other websites may call this API
the part of a web address after a question mark, often holding search terms or values

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and app creation
sections.what: Loads the web framework, the cross-origin helper, the request logger, the route list and the logger, then creates the app object.
sections.why: The app object must exist before any step can be attached to it.
sections.watch_out: The app object is shared by everything that imports it, so changes here affect every request.

sections.name: use
sections.title: Request logging
sections.what: Writes one log entry per request with the method, the address without its query string, and the response status code.
sections.why: Likely reason: the query string is removed so values such as tokens or search terms are not written to the logs.
sections.watch_out: Query values are not logged at all, so debugging a query problem needs another source of information.

sections.name: use
sections.title: Cross-origin permissions
sections.what: Allows web pages served from other addresses to call this API from a browser.
sections.why: Likely reason: the web front end runs on a different address from the API.
sections.watch_out: No options are passed, so every origin is allowed, and this should be narrowed before sensitive data is served.

sections.name: use
sections.title: JSON body reading
sections.what: Reads JSON content sent in request bodies and makes it available to the routes.
sections.why: Some routes, such as starting a run, expect their input as JSON.
sections.watch_out: A malformed JSON body produces an error that this file does not handle itself.

sections.name: use
sections.title: Form body reading
sections.what: Reads form-style request bodies, including nested fields, and makes them available to the routes.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Likely to support form submissions.
sections.watch_out: Nested form data can be larger or more complex, so routes must check their inputs.

sections.name: use
sections.title: Route mounting and export
sections.what: Sends every address that starts with /api to the router, then exports the app so the server start code can run it.
sections.why: Keeps all API routes in one place under one prefix.
sections.watch_out: Any path the router does not match gets the framework default response, because no not-found handler is defined here.

summary: Sets up the Express web server: request logging, cross-origin permissions, reading of JSON and form bodies, and routing of all API paths under /api.
purpose: Builds the web application object that the server start code runs.
why: Likely reason: the order of the steps matters, with logging first, then permissions, then body reading, then routes.
how: Creates the app, attaches the request logger, allows cross-origin calls, reads JSON and form bodies, sends every /api address to the router, and exports the app.
inputs: Incoming HTTP requests, the route list in ./routes, and the logger in ./lib/logger.
outputs: A default-exported app object, plus one log entry per request with the method, the path without the query string, and the status code.
risks: The cross-origin setting allows every website to call the API, and no error handler is added in this file, so unexpected errors use the framework default response.
debug: If requests never reach a route, check the order of the steps. For cross-origin errors in a browser, check the cross-origin setting. If request logs are missing, check the logger setup.
